8ea289b803:
Expected lesion: granulomatous inflammation with caseating granulomas: secondary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis.

Gross

  • Apical or posterior upper-lobe lesion with a cavity lined by yellow-grey, cheesy (caseous) material.
  • Surrounding consolidation, fibrosis and pleural thickening; satellite lesions may spread through the bronchi.

Microscopy

  • Central caseous necrosis: structureless, granular, pink debris (cell outlines lost).
  • Surrounded by epithelioid macrophages (abundant pale cytoplasm, slipper-shaped nuclei).
  • Langhans giant cells with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery.
  • A cuff of lymphocytes, then fibroblasts and fibrosis at the edge.
  • Acid-fast bacilli shown with the Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
18f95366e2:
Whether ischaemia ends as an infarct, and how large it is, depends on:

  • Nature of the blood supply: organs with a dual or collateral supply (lung, liver, hand) resist infarction; end-arterial organs (kidney, spleen) infarct readily.
  • Rate of occlusion: slow narrowing allows collaterals to develop; sudden occlusion does not.
  • Vulnerability of the tissue to hypoxia: neurons die after 3 to 4 minutes and myocardium after 20 to 30 minutes, while fibroblasts survive much longer.
  • Oxygen content of the blood: anaemia, hypoxaemia or heart failure make infarction more likely and larger.
add07c611d:
Provisional diagnosis: septic shock (sepsis with hypotension and multi-organ dysfunction).

Investigations

  • Blood culture (before antibiotics) and culture of the likely source: urine, sputum, wound or CSF.
  • Complete blood count: leukocytosis or leukopenia, thrombocytopenia.
  • Serum lactate (tissue hypoperfusion), CRP and procalcitonin.
  • Coagulation profile: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer (for DIC).
  • Organ function: urea, creatinine and electrolytes, liver function tests, blood glucose, arterial blood gases.
  • Imaging for the source: chest X-ray, ultrasound of the abdomen.
6faddc8cc2:
Most likely diagnosis: septic shock.

Pathogenesis

  • Recognition of microbes: bacterial products (such as endotoxin) bind Toll-like and other receptors on macrophages, neutrophils and endothelium.
  • Cytokine storm: TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 drive fever and a systemic inflammatory response; complement is activated.
  • Vasodilation: nitric oxide and prostaglandins dilate vessels, so blood pressure falls.
  • Endothelial injury: leaky vessels cause oedema and loss of circulating volume.
  • Procoagulant state: tissue factor is expressed, so microthrombi form and DIC can follow.
  • Metabolic changes: insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia, later adrenal insufficiency.
  • Multi-organ failure: hypoperfusion and microthrombi injure the lungs (ARDS), kidneys, liver and brain (loss of consciousness).
b56c2198f5:
Salient features of autosomal dominant disorders

  • A single mutant allele is enough to cause disease.
  • Both sexes are affected with equal frequency, and either parent can pass it on.
  • Vertical transmission: the disease appears in every generation.
  • Each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk.
  • Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity are common.
  • Many cases arise from a new mutation, especially when the disease reduces fertility.
  • Onset is often delayed to adulthood; the mutant genes often code for structural proteins or receptors.
  • Examples: Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolaemia, adult polycystic kidney disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, Huntington disease, hereditary spherocytosis, familial adenomatous polyposis.

Turner syndrome

  • Karyotype: 45,X (complete loss of one X) in most cases; the rest are mosaics or have a structurally abnormal X.
  • Features: short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus and lymphoedema of hands and feet at birth.
  • Heart and kidney: coarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney.
  • Gonads: streak ovaries, causing primary amenorrhoea, infertility and absent secondary sexual characteristics.
  • Intelligence is usually normal; hypothyroidism is common.
  • Diagnosis: karyotyping; buccal smear shows no Barr body.
1b4d379840:
• Dysplasia: disordered growth with loss of uniformity and orientation of cells: pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and mitoses above the basal layer. Example: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, dysplasia in Barrett oesophagus.
  • Carcinoma in situ: dysplastic change through the whole epithelial thickness while the basement membrane remains unbreached, so spread has not yet begun. Example: CIN III (HSIL) of the cervix, ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast.
  • Grading: how differentiated the tumour cells are and how many mitoses they show (well, moderately or poorly differentiated). Examples: Gleason score in prostate cancer, Nottingham grade in breast cancer.
  • Staging: how far the tumour has spread, by the TNM system: size and local extent of the primary (T), lymph node spread (N) and distant metastasis (M). Example: breast carcinoma T2 N1 M0. Stage predicts outcome better than grade.
e5babc0b5f:
Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K.

Functions of vitamin D

  • Increases intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
  • Keeps serum calcium and phosphate high enough for mineralisation of bone (osteoid).
  • With PTH, mobilises calcium from bone by stimulating osteoclast formation (through RANKL) when serum calcium falls.
  • Increases renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.
  • Other roles: suppresses PTH secretion and modulates immunity.
2360cd3649:
Risk factors of IHD

  • Not modifiable: increasing age, male sex, family history and genetic factors.
  • Modifiable: hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus, raised LDL or low HDL cholesterol, obesity and the metabolic syndrome, physical inactivity.
  • Others: raised CRP, lipoprotein(a), hyperhomocysteinaemia.

Cardiac markers raised in MI

  • Cardiac troponin I and T: most sensitive and specific; rise in 2 to 4 hours, stay raised for 7 to 10 days.
  • CK-MB: begins to climb within a few hours, is highest around the first day and is back to baseline by day three, which makes it useful for spotting a second infarct.
  • Myoglobin: rises earliest but is not specific to the heart.
26d96db264:
(a) Probable diagnosis: stable angina pectoris, chest pain on exertion relieved by rest, from coronary atherosclerosis (risk factors: smoking, heavy exertion, family history of sudden cardiac death).

(b) Outcomes if untreated

  • Progression to unstable angina.
  • Acute myocardial infarction.
  • Sudden cardiac death, usually from an arrhythmia.
  • Chronic ischaemic heart disease with progressive heart failure.
  • Arrhythmias.
829322b3dc:
(a) Most likely diagnosis: acute myocardial infarction.

(b) Pathogenesis

  • An atherosclerotic plaque (risk raised by hypertension and diabetes) ruptures or erodes, exposing collagen and the lipid core.
  • Platelets adhere, aggregate and release thromboxane A2, ADP and serotonin, which also cause vasospasm.
  • Tissue factor activates coagulation, and within minutes a thrombus occludes the coronary artery.
  • Ischaemia stops aerobic metabolism: contractility is lost within a minute, and cell injury becomes irreversible after 20 to 40 minutes.
  • Necrosis spreads from the subendocardium outwards as a wavefront and becomes transmural over 3 to 6 hours.

(c) Cardiac biomarkers

  • Troponin I and T (most specific), CK-MB (helps detect re-infarction) and myoglobin (early, not specific).
4e7d325838:
The revised Jones criteria (American Heart Association, 2015) diagnose rheumatic fever.

  • Essential: proof of recent group A streptococcal infection, such as a high or climbing ASO titre, a positive throat swab culture or a positive rapid antigen test.
  • First attack: 2 major criteria, or 1 major and 2 minor.
  • Recurrence: 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, or 3 minor.

Major criteria

  • Carditis (clinical, or subclinical on echocardiography).
  • Arthritis: polyarthritis (in moderate or high-risk populations, monoarthritis or polyarthralgia also count).
  • Sydenham chorea.
  • Erythema marginatum.
  • Subcutaneous nodules.

Minor criteria

  • Polyarthralgia (monoarthralgia in high-risk populations).
  • Fever (38.5 °C, or 38 °C in high-risk populations).
  • Raised ESR (60 mm in the first hour, or 30 in high-risk populations) or CRP (3 mg/dL or more).
  • Prolonged PR interval, unless carditis is already counted.
fe1786461f:
Infective endocarditis: microbial infection of the heart valves or endocardium, usually bacterial, forming bulky, friable vegetations of thrombus and organisms.

Predisposing factors

  • Rheumatic heart disease.
  • Congenital heart disease: VSD, PDA, bicuspid aortic valve.
  • Mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation; degenerative calcific valve disease.
  • Prosthetic valves; previous endocarditis.
  • Intravenous drug use (often the tricuspid valve); indwelling catheters.
  • Dental procedures and poor oral hygiene; diabetes and immunosuppression.

Complications

  • Cardiac: valve destruction and regurgitation, heart failure, ring abscess, conduction block.
  • Embolic: septic infarcts in the brain, kidney and spleen; mycotic aneurysms.
  • Renal: immune complex glomerulonephritis, infarcts.
  • Systemic: septicaemia; Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots.
b938722278:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: acute rheumatic fever after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis (migratory polyarthritis, carditis, raised ASO titre).

(ii) Characteristic cardiac lesion: the Aschoff body, a focus of fibrinoid change surrounded by lymphocytes and Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells, seen in a pancarditis. Small warty vegetations form along the lines of valve closure, and long-term damage leads to chronic rheumatic valve disease, most often mitral stenosis.
b8ac8dfff1:
(a) Comment: the picture suggests tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease), tuberculosis of the spine with constitutional symptoms (evening fever, night sweats, weight loss) in a person from a high-risk background.

(b) Special stain: the Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli (auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain is an alternative). The biopsy also shows caseating granulomas.
1bb746143b:
Probable diagnosis: pulmonary tuberculosis.

Investigations

  • Sputum for acid-fast bacilli (Ziehl-Neelsen stain), two to three samples.
  • GeneXpert MTB/RIF: detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within hours.
  • Sputum culture (Lowenstein-Jensen or liquid culture) with drug sensitivity.
  • Chest X-ray: upper-zone infiltrates or cavities.
  • Complete blood count and ESR (raised ESR, lymphocytosis).
  • Supportive tests: Mantoux (tuberculin) test or an IGRA blood test, and screening for HIV.
66e71fab83:
Tuberculosis is a disease of cell-mediated immunity (type IV hypersensitivity).

  • Entry: inhaled droplet nuclei reach the alveoli and are taken up by macrophages.
  • Early unchecked growth: the bacilli block phagolysosome maturation and multiply for about 3 weeks, spreading through lymphatics and blood (seeding other organs).
  • TH1 response: macrophages present antigen and secrete IL-12, so TH1 cells develop and release interferon-gamma.
  • Macrophage activation: interferon-gamma lets macrophages destroy the bacilli (phagolysosome maturation, nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species).
  • Granuloma formation: TNF recruits monocytes, which become epithelioid cells and giant cells; the centre undergoes caseous necrosis. The tuberculin test becomes positive.
  • Primary TB: Ghon focus plus hilar nodes (Ghon complex), usually healing by fibrosis and calcification.
  • Secondary TB: reactivation or reinfection in a sensitised host, giving apical cavitation.
  • Poor immunity (HIV, malnutrition) allows progressive and miliary disease.
fb6abfcc08:
• Hypercalcaemia: PTH-related peptide, mainly from squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Cushing syndrome: ACTH, from small cell carcinoma.
  • SIADH with hyponatraemia: ADH, from small cell carcinoma.
  • Neuromuscular syndromes: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (antibodies to calcium channels), cerebellar degeneration and sensory neuropathy, mostly with small cell carcinoma.
  • Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy and clubbing, especially with adenocarcinoma.
  • Hypercoagulability: migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), DIC.
  • Others: carcinoid syndrome, gynaecomastia (hCG), acanthosis nigricans, dermatomyositis.
db153e2251:
Etiopathogenesis

  • Cigarette smoking: the main cause, related to pack-years. Carcinogens such as polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines form DNA adducts and cause mutations (TP53, KRAS).
  • Occupational and environmental: asbestos, radon and uranium, arsenic, chromium, nickel, air pollution.
  • Molecular: EGFR mutations and ALK rearrangements, especially in adenocarcinoma of non-smokers.
  • Stepwise change (squamous type): hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, then invasive carcinoma.

Four common carcinomas

  • Adenocarcinoma.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Small cell carcinoma.
  • Large cell carcinoma.
861ad7525b:
(a) Most likely type: squamous cell carcinoma, a central (hilar) tumour strongly linked to smoking. Small cell carcinoma is also central and should be considered.

How to proceed

  • Imaging: chest X-ray, then contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen for the tumour and staging.
  • Tissue diagnosis: sputum cytology; bronchoscopy with biopsy, brushings and washings; EBUS or CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral or nodal lesions.
  • Histopathology with immunohistochemistry: p40/p63 (squamous), TTF-1 and napsin A (adenocarcinoma), chromogranin and synaptophysin (small cell).
  • Molecular tests in non-small cell carcinoma: EGFR, ALK, PD-L1.
  • Staging: PET-CT, MRI of the brain, bone scan as needed.
44a4a1b9a8:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: bronchogenic carcinoma (heavy smoker with cough, haemoptysis and weight loss; hoarseness suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement).

(ii) Diagnostic approach

  • Imaging: chest X-ray, then contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen for the tumour and staging.
  • Tissue diagnosis: sputum cytology; bronchoscopy with biopsy, brushings and washings; EBUS or CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral or nodal lesions.
  • Histopathology with immunohistochemistry: p40/p63 (squamous), TTF-1 and napsin A (adenocarcinoma), chromogranin and synaptophysin (small cell).
  • Molecular tests in non-small cell carcinoma: EGFR, ALK, PD-L1.
  • Staging: PET-CT, MRI of the brain, bone scan as needed.
94c5f93a24:
Sialadenitis: inflammation of a salivary gland. Causes include viruses (mumps), bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, often with dehydration or duct obstruction), duct stones (sialolithiasis) and autoimmune disease (Sjogren syndrome).

Classification of salivary gland tumours

  • Benign epithelial: pleomorphic adenoma (the commonest), Warthin tumour, basal cell adenoma, oncocytoma, myoepithelioma.
  • Malignant epithelial: mucoepidermoid carcinoma (the commonest malignant), adenoid cystic carcinoma, acinic cell carcinoma, carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, salivary duct carcinoma.
  • Non-epithelial: haemangioma, lymphangioma, lymphoma.
42fe448d62:
Gastritis: inflammation of the gastric mucosa.

Classification

  • Acute: NSAIDs, alcohol, severe stress (burns, shock), uraemia, chemotherapy, ischaemia.
  • Chronic: Helicobacter pylori gastritis (mainly antrum); autoimmune gastritis (body and fundus); others: chemical (reactive) gastropathy from bile reflux or NSAIDs, lymphocytic, eosinophilic and granulomatous gastritis.

Aetiopathogenesis of chronic gastritis

  • H. pylori: flagella and adhesins let it live in the mucus layer; urease makes ammonia that buffers acid and injures cells; CagA and VacA drive inflammation and cell damage.
  • Autoimmune: antibodies and T cells against parietal cells (the proton pump) and intrinsic factor destroy the oxyntic glands, causing achlorhydria, vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia) and high gastrin.

Morphology

  • Lymphocytes and plasma cells in the lamina propria; neutrophils in the glands when active.
  • Lymphoid follicles and curved bacilli in the surface mucus in H. pylori gastritis.
  • Gland loss (atrophy) and intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells, sometimes dysplasia.
  • Autoimmune type: diffuse atrophy of the body and fundus with neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia.
5d3af06250:
Peptic ulcer disease: a chronic breach of the lining that goes deeper than the muscularis mucosae, in parts of the gut bathed by acid and pepsin. Usual sites: the proximal duodenum (commonest) and the gastric antrum along the lesser curve; less often the distal oesophagus, a Meckel diverticulum or the jejunum in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Pathogenesis

An imbalance between damaging and protective forces.

  • Damaging: H. pylori infection (the commonest cause), NSAIDs (block prostaglandin synthesis), acid and pepsin, smoking, high gastrin (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
  • Protective: mucus and bicarbonate, tight junctions between epithelial cells, mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins, rapid epithelial renewal.
  • H. pylori raises acid output (fewer somatostatin cells, more gastrin), colonises gastric metaplasia in the duodenum and injures the mucosa with urease, toxins and the inflammation it provokes.

Diseases associated with H. pylori

  • Chronic (antral-predominant) gastritis.
  • Peptic ulcer, duodenal and gastric.
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma.
  • Gastric MALT lymphoma.
  • Associated with iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.
b41133f835:
Diseases associated with H. pylori

  • Chronic (antral-predominant) gastritis.
  • Peptic ulcer, duodenal and gastric.
  • Gastric adenocarcinoma.
  • Gastric MALT lymphoma.
  • Associated with iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

Role of H. pylori in peptic ulcer

  • More acid: antral gastritis reduces somatostatin-producing D cells, so gastrin and acid output rise.
  • Duodenal colonisation: acid causes gastric metaplasia in the duodenum, which the organism then colonises, causing duodenitis and ulcer.
  • Direct injury: urease produces ammonia; proteases and phospholipases weaken the mucus layer; CagA and VacA damage epithelial cells and trigger IL-8 release.
  • Host inflammation: neutrophils and their reactive oxygen species add to mucosal damage.
  • Eradicating H. pylori heals ulcers and prevents them coming back.
4186e1bd1b:
• Distribution: Crohn disease can affect any part of the gut (most often the terminal ileum) with skip lesions; ulcerative colitis involves the rectum and spreads continuously upwards through the colon.
  • Depth: Crohn inflammation is transmural, causing fissures, fistulae and strictures; ulcerative colitis is limited to the mucosa and submucosa.
  • Granulomas: non-caseating granulomas are seen in Crohn disease, not in ulcerative colitis.
  • Also: cobblestone mucosa, creeping fat and perianal disease favour Crohn disease.
d619401442:
Two major pathways

  • APC / beta-catenin (chromosomal instability) pathway: the adenoma-carcinoma sequence; loss of APC, then KRAS activation, then loss of TP53 and SMAD4. About 80% of cases.
  • Microsatellite instability pathway: defective DNA mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2), as in Lynch syndrome, and the serrated pathway with BRAF mutation and gene hypermethylation.

Risk factors

  • Diet low in fibre and high in red and processed meat; obesity and inactivity.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease; adenomatous polyps; family history and hereditary syndromes (FAP, Lynch syndrome).
1d535923be:
• Non-neoplastic: hyperplastic polyp; inflammatory polyp (pseudopolyps of IBD); hamartomatous polyps (juvenile polyp, Peutz-Jeghers polyp); lymphoid polyp.
  • Neoplastic: adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous); serrated lesions (sessile serrated lesion, traditional serrated adenoma).
  • Polyposis syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis (with Gardner and Turcot variants), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis, Cowden syndrome.
  • In the stomach: fundic gland polyps, hyperplastic polyps, adenomas. Submucosal tumours (lipoma, GIST, neuroendocrine tumour) can also present as polyps.
e8be1bb5c2:
Classification of intestinal polyps

  • Non-neoplastic: hyperplastic polyp; inflammatory polyp (pseudopolyps of IBD); hamartomatous polyps (juvenile polyp, Peutz-Jeghers polyp); lymphoid polyp.
  • Neoplastic: adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous); serrated lesions (sessile serrated lesion, traditional serrated adenoma).
  • Polyposis syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis (with Gardner and Turcot variants), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, juvenile polyposis, Cowden syndrome.
  • In the stomach: fundic gland polyps, hyperplastic polyps, adenomas. Submucosal tumours (lipoma, GIST, neuroendocrine tumour) can also present as polyps.

Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome)

  • Autosomal dominant; a germline mutation in a DNA mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2), causing microsatellite instability.
  • Colorectal cancer at a young age, often right-sided, with few polyps (not polyposis); tumours are often mucinous with many tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes and have a better prognosis.
  • Other cancers: endometrium (the commonest), ovary, stomach, small bowel, urinary tract, hepatobiliary tract, brain and sebaceous skin tumours.
  • Diagnosis: Amsterdam criteria or Bethesda guidelines, tumour testing (MMR immunohistochemistry, MSI) and germline testing.
  • Management: colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years from age 20 to 25; screening for endometrial cancer.
8c1725d5a0:
(a) Most likely diagnosis: colorectal carcinoma, probably right-sided (caecum or ascending colon), which typically bleeds slowly and presents with iron deficiency anaemia in an older patient.

(b) Most important investigation: colonoscopy with biopsy for histopathological confirmation, followed by CT for staging and serum CEA as a baseline.
